data.abstractNote: This paper shows the status quaestionis about some aspects of the old Syriac version of the Gospels. The Syriac Church used two ways to spread the Gospels: Tatianus' Diatessaron (175 a. C.), and the Mepharreshe, that is the Separated Gospels, handed down by two manuscripts, the Curetonian and the Syrosinaiticus, dated IV-V century. In the most diffused present opinion the two manuscripts can be two different recensions of the Old Syriac version. The Syrosinaiticus seems to be the oldest witness in spite of a long transmission process. The Old Syriac version is generally considered later and partly depending on the Diatessaron; it can go back to the early III century even if some questions are still unsolved. Such a version shows some traces of expressions deriving from various authors differently and it is the subject of one of the most interesting debates about the origins of Christianity.

data.title: Transformations in Minority Religious Leadership: The Yezidis, Shabak, and Assyrians in Northern Iraq
data.abstractNote: This paper discusses three religious communities in Northern Iraq that are characterized by the shared fate of having been targeted by the 2014 “Islamic State” (IS) offensive. These events dramatically brought home the vulnerability of these communities in post-Saddam Iraq; but the precarious status of these groups was already painfully visible even to the most casual observer prior to the IS onslaught. In this paper, I trace the rather different trajectories of these—initially broadly comparable—minority groups, with a focus on the changing articulation and legitimation of religious leadership. I do so by pointing out some of the longer-term tendencies among these groups, while treating religious leadership in terms of patronage.

data.title: Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia, and the Interpretation of the Messianic Psalms
data.abstractNote: For the majority of the patristic tradition, the Psalms are full of prophetic references to Christ, justified by New Testament citations and creative reading strategies. But for two writers from the so-called Antiochene school, Diodore of Tarsus and his student Theodore of Mopsuestia, this is not the case; New Testament use of the Old Testament is not prescriptive and allegory must be avoided at all costs. Diodore and Theodore only recognize four psalms as messianic: Ps 2, 8, 45, and 110. But not only do both theologians read Christ into these psalms, they do so in a manner that is unusual compared to how they approach the rest of the Psalter. This essay seeks to shed light on the reasons underlying these seeming exceptions. Pushing back against the now outdated paradigm of the Antiochene school as purely historical or literal exegesis, this essay will argue that both Diodore and Theodore are motivated not primarily by exegetical method, but more so by theological and textual concerns. More specifically, the readings of these four psalms are shaped by the Antiochene Christological vision found in Heb 1–2, which results in the prioritization of this text over the psalms in question.

data.title: The Doctrine of New Creation in the Theology of John Wesley
data.abstractNote: The purpose of this dissertation is to clarify the doctrine of new creation in the theology of John Wesley. And the basic assumption that guides my inquiry is that there can be a new hermeneutical clue--a transformative, dynamic teleology of re-creation--which helps to re-read Wesley’s theology. According to this re-reading, Wesley views the true nature of Christian religion as the restoration of the image and likeness of God. This larger scheme overcomes the tendency toward an individualistic reading of salvation that results from an interpretation of Wesley based on the ordo salutis. After clarifying the centrality of a dynamic teleology, the implications for Wesley’s religious epistemology are discussed. Seen in this wider context, the ‘spiritual senses’ function as a medium through which we grasp the true revelation of God’s love. Whether obscured or lost because of the Fall, these new senses are awakened by the Spirit of God in the new birth. But the final goal of this spiritual apprehension is the perfection of our potential in terms of the entire renewal and sanctification in the image and likeness of God. Finally, the historical sources of Wesley’s dynamic teleology of new creation are investigated. Foremost for this inquiry is his reading of the Macarian homilies that reflect the early Syriac tradition. Against Outler’s opinion that Gregory of Nyssa is the prime influence on Wesley’s concept of perfection (teleiosis), this dissertation argues that Macarius and the Syriac tradition deserve proper recognition as a major source for what is distinctive in Wesley’s understanding of perfection, sanctification, and the spiritual senses. In the theology of Macarius, we find a great many parallels to Wesley’s teleological orientation that enables us to regard it as a presupposed substructure for the Wesleyan synthesis. As a result, Wesley’s theology is connected to primitive Christianity through the ancient Syriac tradition.
